title: 7 Rules of the Roman Jurists
dek: Working maxims of the lawyers whose method shaped European law

slides.heading: Law Is an Art, Not Code
slides.body: The *Digest* opens with Ulpian quoting Celsus: ius est ars boni et aequi, law is the art of the good and the fair. A jurist was judged on skilled judgement, not on memorising statutes.

art.title: Feather quill rests on an old handwritten ledger

slides.heading: Three Precepts of Law
slides.body: The *Digest* attributes to Ulpian three precepts of law: live honourably, harm no one, give each his due. Justinian's *Institutes* repeated the formula in 533, and it passed into medieval and early modern legal teaching.

art.title: Marble bust of a bearded man with dramatic lighting

slides.heading: Distrust Every Definition
slides.body: Javolenus warned that every definition in civil law is dangerous, because it can rarely withstand a hard case. Fritz Schulz, in *History of Roman Legal Science*, stresses that Roman jurists reasoned from concrete cases first.

slides.heading: Ignorance of Law Is No Excuse
slides.body: Paul states the rule plainly: ignorance of law harms you, ignorance of fact does not. Roman law did allow exceptions, notably for minors, soldiers and in some cases women. The modern maxim descends from here.

slides.heading: Give Answers When Consulted
slides.body: Jurists built authority through responsa, opinions given to citizens and magistrates. Pomponius says Augustus granted some a right to answer with his authority. Its exact scope is debated; Bruce Frier traces the profession's rise in *The Rise of the Roman Jurists*.

art.title: Statue of roman emperor augustus points upward

slides.heading: Sort Law Into Three
slides.body: Gaius divided all law into persons, things and actions. His *Institutes* survived in a Verona palimpsest identified in 1816. Peter Stein shows how this scheme shaped later civil codes across Europe.

slides.heading: When Jurists Disagree, Count
slides.body: The Law of Citations of 426 named five authorities: Papinian, Paul, Ulpian, Gaius, Modestinus. Judges followed the majority; on a tie, Papinian prevailed. Scholars often read it as a symptom of post-classical decline.

art.title: a wooden shelf filled with lots of books

caption:
Roman jurists distrusted definitions.
Historians such as Stein trace their influence on later European legal thought. The *Digest* keeps their working rules: law as the art of the good and the fair (Celsus, quoted by Ulpian), every definition is dangerous (Javolenus), ignorance of law no excuse (Paul). Their method grew from cases, not codes (Schulz 1946; Frier 1985). Gaius's three-part scheme outlived the empire (Stein 1999).

risk_notes: Ius respondendi: its nature and whether Augustus created a formal privilege is debated (Pomponius is the main source). Keep 'Pomponius says' and the Contested flag.
Ignorantia iuris: Roman law had exceptions (minors, soldiers, women in certain cases, rustici in some texts). Keep the Simplified flag and mention the exceptions.

Law of Citations as 'decline': this is an interpretation, linked to Schulz's view of post-classical law. Phrase as 'often read as', not as fact. It is an imperial constitution, not a jurist's maxim, which is why the title refers to the jurists collectively.
Gaius palimpsest: identified by Niebuhr at Verona in 1816. Avoid saying 'discovered' as if the manuscript itself was unknown.

Three precepts: Ulpian only says 'iuris praecepta sunt haec', and some scholars question whether the wording is his own or the compilers'. The slide says 'the Digest attributes to Ulpian'; keep that phrasing if challenged.
Ius est ars boni et aequi: the definition is Celsus's, quoted by Ulpian ('ut eleganter Celsus definit'). Never attribute it to Ulpian alone.

issues.problem: "Roman jurists distrusted definitions." turns one jurist's maxim (Javolenus, D.50.17.202) into a claim about all Roman jurists. The post itself contradicts it: slide 1 and the caption open with Celsus's definition of law, quoted approvingly by Ulpian. Gaius also opens his Institutes with definitions. A commenter will point this out.
issues.fix: Change to: "One Roman jurist warned that every definition is dangerous." Or: "Javolenus warned that every definition in civil law is dangerous."

issues.problem: "shaped later civil codes across Europe" is too broad. The Gaian persons, things and actions scheme shaped institutional-style codes such as the French Code civil and the Austrian ABGB. The German BGB follows the Pandectist scheme with a general part instead, so the claim does not hold for every European code.
issues.fix: Change to: "Peter Stein shows how this scheme shaped later civil codes, including the French Code civil." This keeps the body at about 32 words.

issues.problem: The Law of Citations is an imperial constitution issued by Theodosius II and Valentinian III, not a rule made by the jurists. The heading "When Jurists Disagree, Count" sits under the title "Rules of the Roman Jurists", so readers may take it as the jurists' own rule.
issues.fix: Start the body with: "An imperial law, the Law of Citations of 426, named five authorities: ..." Shorten the last sentence if needed to stay at 40 words or fewer.
